Original P13.2 (T4): The image of the ﬁxed-Reeb Monge–Ampère operator
Characterize precisely the image of MAξ : E 1 (ξ)/R → M1 (ξ) and the measures admitting a
solution. Retain the invariant carrier X0T and the aﬃne-cone probability normalization. The
operator is already bi-Lipschitz onto its image, so uniqueness there is established; the residual
is the image and existence characterization.


Complete unchanged mathematical family:

7     Finite-energy equations on polarized aﬃne cones
Active items: P13.1, P13.2. Status: Open in the residual scope.

7.1   Atomic targets
P13.1 (T4): Comparison for nonproportional Reeb polarizations
For a normal polarized aﬃne cone (X, T ; ξ) over an algebraically closed trivially valued
characteristic-zero ﬁeld, compare PSH(ξ) and PSH(ξ 0 ) for nonproportional Reeb ﬁelds. Ob-
tain the estimates strong enough for uniform diﬀerentiability of energy. Identities along one
proportional Reeb ray do not answer this question.

P13.2 (T4): The image of the ﬁxed-Reeb Monge–Ampère operator
Characterize precisely the image of MAξ : E 1 (ξ)/R → M1 (ξ) and the measures admitting a
solution. Retain the invariant carrier X0T and the aﬃne-cone probability normalization. The
operator is already bi-Lipschitz onto its image, so uniqueness there is established; the residual
is the image and existence characterization.

7.2   What constitutes a solution
For P13.1 the estimates must compare nonproportional Reeb ﬁelds and have the uniformity
actually needed for energy diﬀerentiation. For P13.2 state necessary and suﬃcient condi-
tions on measures on the invariant carrier, respecting the existing probability convention;
bi-Lipschitzness onto the image does not imply surjectivity.

7.3   Full statement and detailed state of the art
Problem 7.1. Let (X, T ; ξ) be a normal polarized aﬃne cone over an algebraically closed
trivially valued ﬁeld of characteristic zero. Develop a comparison calculus for PSH(ξ) and
PSH(ξ 0 ) when ξ and ξ 0 are nonproportional Reeb ﬁelds, strong enough to prove the required
uniform diﬀerentiability of the energy. For a ﬁxed ξ, characterize the image of

                                  MAξ : E 1 (ξ)/R −→ M1 (ξ),

and determine exactly which µ ∈ M1 (ξ) admit a solution of MAξ (ϕ) = µ, unique modulo
constants.

    The ﬁxed-polarization theory is already substantial: Book Theorem 70.9.1 constructs the
mixed operator, proves decreasing-net continuity, and makes the single-potential operator bi-
Lipschitz onto its image. Here M1 (ξ) uses the invariant carrier X0T of Book Deﬁnition 70.9.1:
all aﬃne-cone psh functions factor through toriﬁcation, and all canonical model and ﬁnite-
energy measures are supported on that closed carrier. A measure on the full link outside X0T
cannot be an output; energy tests see only its toriﬁcation. Thus the remaining image problem
concerns ﬁnite-energy measures on X0T , with the aﬃne-cone probability normalization (Book
70.62) explicitly retained. The proportional-rescaling identities of [Wu24, Proposition 3.3]
do not compare nonproportional Reeb rays. Rational approximation likewise does not yield
constants uniform in two varying polarizations. The available arXiv source is still version 1
at this cutoﬀ. Its “Outlook and relation to other works” identiﬁes uniform diﬀerentiability as
the key missing input and locates it in understanding PSH(ξ) versus PSH(ξ 0 ) when the Reeb
ﬁelds are not multiples [Wu24]. It therefore supplies neither a cross-polarization estimate nor
surjectivity onto M1 (ξ).


                                               64

    The natural strategy is to prove Reeb-uniform Hodge-index and I–J estimates on a com-
pact slice of the Reeb cone, use them to diﬀerentiate the energy along rational approximants,
and then run the ﬁnite-energy variational method. At present the ﬁrst step is unavailable: the
known addition formula stays on one Reeb ray, and an irrational output measure may already
be carried by a genuinely quasimonomial point. No argument in this edition closes either
the cross-polarization estimate or the image characterization. Both residuals are therefore
open and are recorded as one coupled, unresolved Rethlas packet in the editorial ledger; no
veriﬁcation verdict is claimed for either residual.

# Fiberwise zero class and finite-data envelope descent

Status: new root proposal, not independently reviewed, not an accepted dependency. No original problem is closed by this record. The active original author campaigns P16.1 round 72 and P13.2 round 73 retain their frozen inputs; no hot feedback has been sent.

This proposal concerns projective varieties over algebraically closed trivially valued fields of characteristic zero, with an ample rational line bundle. It does not assert the discrete or arbitrary complete field versions of P16.1/P16.4. Auxiliary complete extensions below are used only to compare values of an already genuine pulled-back metric. They do not supply an affine regularization theorem over arbitrary completed residue fields.

## 1. Exact antecedents and separation of gates

F1. For the genuine metric definition being used, a bounded pi*L-psh metric admits decreasing genuine approximants in pi*L + epsilon A, where A is a fixed ample line bundle with an actual semipositive reference metric, epsilon is positive rational and decreases to zero. Pullback of these actual metrics through complete field extension and to an algebraic smooth projective curve preserves their local logarithmic-section subharmonicity. A bounded floor max(u,M), relative to the actual pullback reference, remains genuine. This is a metric assertion, with the actual reference and classes identified; a numerical nef class alone is not a substitute.

F2. Smooth nef envelope theory is available upstairs. Genuine psh functions there are minimum usc extensions from divisorial valuations, and a bounded supremum has unchanged values on that set after usc regularization. The finite morphism from the normalization of X is a universal homeomorphism; pi has geometrically connected fibers.

C1. Over every countable algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, the preceding singular Runge argument proves weak/genuine local equality and global membership for the descended envelope in the original ample class. This remains the main singular analytic gate. A conditional fiber lemma does not establish C1.

C2. The genuine ample-class theory has decreasing finite Hdom majorants, uniform closure for continuous metrics, decreasing and varying-class closure, the usual PL separation/density, and actual pullback through ground-field extension. C3. The actual continuous mixed MA operator is positive, has raw total mass V=(L^n), and commutes with ground-field extension by pushforward. ## 3. A direct bounded zero-class fiber lemma

Claim, under F1: let F be a complete characteristic-zero field and Y a projective geometrically connected F-scheme. Suppose that a bounded usc function w on Y^an is supplied by a genuine metric on a line bundle trivialized over all of Y, and that the approximants and all base changes/restrictions specified in F1 apply. Then w is constant. We work on Y_red, which has the same analytic points and function values; we do not discard cycle multiplicities in any later MA calculation.

Here is the value comparison, including arbitrary analytic points rather than merely a dense subset. Fix one closed point b of Y_red. For any a in Y^an, embed the finite residue field k(b) into a completed algebraic closure K of H(a). If that field is trivially valued, first extend H(a) to H(a)((T)) with its T-adic absolute value and then take the completed algebraic closure. K is now algebraically closed, complete and nontrivially valued. The H(a)-rational point representing a gives a K-rational lift a', and the chosen embedding gives a K-rational lift b'. Pullback keeps the values w(a')=w(a) and w(b')=w(b).

The scheme (Y_K)_red is connected. Its finitely many irreducible components have a connected intersection graph. Resolve each component projectively, in characteristic zero. The resolutions are smooth projective irreducible K-varieties. Every K-point of a component has a K-point preimage on its resolution: its fiber is nonempty and proper, and K is algebraically closed.

On a smooth projective irreducible K-variety, any two K-points can be joined by a connected chain of smooth projective curves. For positive dimension choose sufficiently high very ample complete intersections through the prescribed finite set, using characteristic-zero Bertini with assigned points; dimension one uses the variety itself, and dimension zero has just one point. Equivalently one can use a finite chain after resolving the selected curves. This algebraic curve-joining statement is an explicit external geometric premise requiring source verification, not an analytic density assertion.

Along every such smooth projective curve C, the pulled-back line bundle from Y is globally trivial and its chosen reference is flat. In a local frame of A let h be the continuous semipositive reference weight. The F1 approximants have local subharmonic weights

    w_i + epsilon_i h,

where w_i decreases to w and epsilon_i decreases to zero. On a relatively compact frame domain, adding a fixed constant to h makes h nonnegative. It then preserves the decreasing order of these local weights. Actual sections give subharmonic logarithmic weights, and finite positive maxima preserve subharmonicity. Thuillier 3.1.8(ii) applies to their decreasing limit. The limit is w, and boundedness excludes the identically negative-infinity alternative. This proves local subharmonicity on C; it assumes the exact F1 reference identification and does not infer it from abstract numerical pullback.

C^an is compact and connected and is a strict smooth analytic curve over K. The bounded usc function w attains a finite maximum M. Thuillier 3.1.11 makes it locally constant near every point where it equals M. The set {w=M} is closed by upper semicontinuity, open by that strong maximum principle, and nonempty. Thus w=M on C^an.

Values consequently agree at the two chosen points on each resolved component, and at closed points of every nonempty intersection of adjacent components. The connected intersection graph gives w(a')=w(b'). Since a was arbitrary, w(a)=w(b) everywhere. Comparing actual values after extension is essential: equality merely on a dense set would not determine an arbitrary usc function.

For the fiber of pi over x in X^an, the line bundle pi*L is the pullback of the one-dimensional H(x)-space L_x. Its reference norm is constant on that entire fiber, so the zero-class trivialization used above is literal. First apply the argument to u_M=max(u,M). Without this floor, a whole component or fiber might carry negative infinity, and the subharmonic definition would not apply. Geometric connectedness is retained under the auxiliary extensions. Each u_M is constant on the fiber. Letting M decrease to negative infinity proves that u itself is constant there, with the value negative infinity allowed.

## 4. Proper birational descent without the flat-stratum lift assertion

Apply section 3 to a genuine upstairs u. Define v(x) to be its common fiber value. Properness and compactness make pi^an closed, and

    {v >= c} = pi^an({u >= c})

for every real c. Hence v is usc and u=v o pi^an. If x is any point and z is any point above it, F2 expresses u(z) as the upper limit of its divisorial values near z. Because pi is birational between integral varieties, its function fields agree. A nonzero divisorial valuation upstairs therefore restricts to the same divisorial valuation downstairs. Thus

    v(x) = u(z) <= limsup_{y -> x, y in X_div} v(y) <= v(x).

This establishes the minimum usc extension property of v. Here the assertion about images of divisorial valuations uses birationality. It is not asserted for arbitrary proper surjective maps.

This avoids Wu LF 605--610's inference that every prescribed net of base divisorial points can be lifted to a convergent net of source divisorial points merely from openness and density. For a bounded-above family {v_i} in PSH_L(X), let

    u = (sup_i pi* v_i)*

on Z. The class pi*L is nef; F2 makes u genuinely pi*L-psh. The family contains a genuine member, so the envelope remains generically finite; this concerns nonidentical negative infinity on irreducible components, not a claim of finiteness at every analytic point. Section 3 gives a descended usc v. At downstairs divisorial points the birational lift is the same valuation, and F2 gives v=sup_i v_i there.

Since every v_i <= v, upper regularization gives (sup_i v_i)* <= v. Conversely v is the minimum usc extension of those divisorial values, while (sup_i v_i)* is usc and majorizes them. Thus v <= (sup_i v_i)*. Equality follows. The proper resolution witnesses weak membership of v in local frames of L. Under C1 the singular local/global argument supplies genuine PSH_L(X), proving countable-field EP. These last genuine-membership steps remain conditional on C1, not on the fiber lemma alone.

No arbitrary PSH competitor is said to descend to one field. Let q be any genuine L-psh competitor with q<=f. By C2 there is a decreasing directed net of finite continuous Hdom majorants h_j tending pointwise to q. For epsilon>0 the closed sets

## 1. The resolution has geometrically connected fibers

Let nu: Xn -> X be the normalization and p: Z -> Xn a projective resolution. Finite-type schemes over a field have finite normalization. Geometric unibranchness makes nu a universal homeomorphism; this is [Stacks, Tag 0GIQ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GIQ), with its local normalization-ring proof read. For normal X the same conclusion follows from the local normal-domain definition; see [Tag 0BQ3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BQ3).

Apply [Tag 0AY8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AY8) to p. The target Xn is normal and integral, Z is integral and reduced, p is proper, its generic point dominates the target, and the birational generic fiber is Spec k(Xn), whose global functions are exactly k(Xn). All six hypotheses are therefore satisfied. Stein factorization gives geometrically connected fibers of p. The finite intermediate algebra is a reduced integral algebra with the same function field as Xn; normality forces it to equal O_Xn.

For any field-valued point x of X, the normalization fiber is a finite universal-homeomorphism scheme over k(x). Its reduction is a single point with a purely inseparable residue extension. In characteristic zero that extension is the identity. After any further field extension the same conclusion holds. The reduced fiber of pi=nu p consequently has the same underlying space as the corresponding p fiber. Nilpotent thickenings do not change analytic points. Thus pi has geometrically connected fibers also over arbitrary completed residue fields H(x). This concerns fiber topology; it does not discard multiplicities in the MA fundamental cycle.

## 2. Joining two values uses ordinary Bertini on a blowup

Let K be algebraically closed of characteristic zero and Y smooth projective irreducible over K, of dimension d. To compare values at two K-points a,b, equality is immediate if a=b or d=0; for d=1 use Y itself. Assume d>=2 and a!=b.

Blow up the two distinct smooth points. The resulting Y' is smooth projective irreducible. Its exceptional divisors Ea and Eb are projective (d-1)-spaces. Choose a very ample H on Y'. Successively choose d-1 general members of H, keeping every intermediate intersection smooth and connected and meeting each exceptional divisor properly. Ordinary smooth Bertini applies because the complete linear system generates H and embeds Y'; its exact hypotheses and the dimension-count proof are [Tag 0FD6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FD6). At each stage of dimension at least two, connectedness follows from depth at least two, properness and ampleness in [Tag 0FD9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FD9). Smooth connected schemes over K are irreducible here. The combined argument is also recorded in [Tag 0G4G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0G4G).

The additional proper-intersection requirements exclude only finitely many proper closed subsets of each hyperplane parameter space, so they can be imposed with the smoothness requirements. The final C is a smooth projective connected curve. Because H restricts amply to each Ei,

    length(C intersection Ei) = (H^(d-1) . Ei) > 0.

It therefore has a K-point above a and another above b. The composed algebraic morphism C -> Y joins the original points. No linear system with assigned base points was used.

For a connected reduced projective scheme, resolve its finitely many irreducible components, choose preimages of the two points and of closed points in adjacent component intersections, and apply this construction on each resolution. Its component-intersection graph is connected, so finitely many curve comparisons connect the two values. The curves need only map to the original scheme. Consequently F1 must mean pullback of supplied actual metric approximants along algebraic morphisms from smooth curves, including the resolution and blowup maps; it must not be read as just restriction along smooth closed embeddings. Pullback of actual generating sections preserves generation and supplies that functorial route once F1's metric/class identification has been proved.

Let k0 be the algebraic closure in k of a field generated by finitely many coefficients of X, L and a finite PL test. It is countable. ## 4. A finite birational normalization is an actual blowup

This provides a concrete route into BJ's birational PSH theorem after EP, not a substitute for EP. Let B=nu_*O_Xn. It is a finite O_X-algebra inside the common rational function field. Hence Bl_I X is exactly Xn, compatibly on overlaps. This makes the ideal needed for the error-term argument explicit, without changing the variety or passing to a different hull.

## 1. A polynomial norm law exists without flatness

Let A be a normal finitely generated domain over a characteristic-zero field, let B be a finite integral A-algebra which is a domain, and put F=Frac(A), L=Frac(B), d=[L:F]. Finite dominance makes B torsion-free over A. Choose algebra generators b1,...,bm which also generate B as an A-module, adding 1 if needed. Form

    N(T1,...,Tm) = Norm_(L/F)(sum_i Ti bi).

This is homogeneous of degree d. Because L/F is separable, over an algebraic closure of F it is the product of the d conjugate linear forms. Every conjugate bi is integral over A. which is harmonic by Thuillier 2.3.21 (S6 LF3587--3624). It satisfies $b\ge h_x$ nearby and equality at $x$.

To prove subharmonicity without a current pullback, let $h$ be any harmonic function and suppose $b-h$ has a local maximum $M$ at $x$. On a sufficiently small neighborhood,
$$h_x-h\le b-h\le M,\qquad (h_x-h)(x)=M.$$
The harmonic maximum principle, Thuillier 3.1.1 (S6 LF3730--3741), makes $h_x-h$ constant $M$ on a smaller neighborhood. The two inequalities then force $b-h=M$ there. Thus $b-h$ satisfies the strong local maximum principle for every harmonic $h$. Thuillier 3.1.12 (S6 LF3885--3896) says exactly that a finite continuous function with this property is subharmonic. This proves the lemma on arbitrary local analytic curves, without extending their maps globally or replacing analytic units by algebraic functions.

For a finite-floor maximum of positive logarithms, Thuillier 3.1.6 and 3.1.8 give the same conclusion, including zeros. Alternatively the finite-chart construction of Section 2 reduces it to Lemma 3.1. Frame changes add harmonic unit logarithms.

The order for a local decreasing sequence is precise. First pull back every finite continuous contact approximant, on the inverse image of one common neighborhood. Each is subharmonic by the lemma. Then take the pointwise decreasing limit. Thuillier 3.1.8(ii), S6 LF3810--3818, gives on each connected component either a subharmonic limit or the identically $-\infty$ function. A local lower bound excludes that alternative for bounded inputs. No uniform convergence to an upper semicontinuous discontinuous limit is asserted. In a later radial argument an identically $-\infty$ component is treated directly.

A useful but conditional variant is worth recording carefully. If actual varying-class metric approximants restrict to weights $u_i+\epsilon_i h$, with $u_i\downarrow u$, $\epsilon_i\downarrow0$, and a fixed continuous local reference $h$, shift $h$ by a fixed constant to make it nonnegative on a relatively compact domain. These weights then decrease to $u$. This proves restriction once that **actual reference identification** is supplied. Numerical convergence of classes alone does not supply it.

## 4. The actual strict cover, frames, and original cocycle

**Theorem 4.1.** Let $k$ be algebraically closed and trivially valued, $X$ a reduced irreducible projective $k$-variety, and $L$ an ample rational line bundle. Suppose an actual globally glued continuous metric on $L$ has unit-chart rational contact weights, allowing the finite-floor charts of Section 2. Then this metric is a genuine continuous $L$-psh metric, obtained by uniform approximation by genuine FS metrics on the same $L$. Smoothness, countability, and geometric unibranchness are not required in this partial theorem.

**Strict neighborhoods.** On an original affine frame chart, a basic neighborhood of a seminorm is specified by finitely many upper and lower bounds on regular functions. Choose finite rational bounds strictly around the finite nonzero evaluations. At a zero choose only a finite positive upper bound. Invert only functions for which a positive lower bound is imposed. Add finite upper bounds on original affine generators and on these inverses. The weak-inequality bounds form a compact analytic domain with the tested point in its interior and contained in the specified neighborhood. It is a domain in a finite-radius closed affine polydisc with Laurent constraints. Finitely many such compact neighborhoods cover $X^{\rm an}$; shrink them into the specified frame and contact charts. Unit logarithms are bounded above and below on each.

Choose $K=k((\varpi))$, $|\varpi|=e^{-1/Q}$, with $Q$ divisible by the finitely many rational threshold denominators. This is a complete nontrivially valued DVR field with residue field $k$. The chosen polydiscs and Laurent constraints become **strict** $K$-analytic domains after base change. We do not invoke a strict-space theorem over the original trivial field.

**Finite branch domains.** On one such compact strict domain the unit logarithmic image is a finite rational polytope complex by published Ducros Theorem 3.2, S9 LF2077--2155. Its proof first reduces to algebraic rational domains by approximation that leaves norm images unchanged, then uses the valued-field image theorem; its dimension conclusion is only $\le\dim X$. Refine the finite complex by all equality hyperplanes of the selected affine expressions. On each relative open convex cell, different expression classes have distinct values everywhere. Continuity of the selection makes its expression class locally constant; connectedness of the cell makes it constant. Continuity extends that affine value to the closed cell.

Every closed-cell preimage is defined by finitely many rational affine inequalities in unit logs. The finitely many cell constants are rational multiples of the value-group generator. After one finite ramified extension $K'=k((\tau))$, $\varpi=\tau^e$, and clearing integer denominators, each inequality is of the form

The original finite compact neighborhood cover is a G-cover because its interiors cover. This is the finite quasi-net criterion, not a claim that every individual closed cell is a neighborhood. The refinements are finite strict analytic domain covers with actual analytic units.

### 4.2. Exact Gauss coefficient cutoff and descent

Give $K'$ its rational step $h=-\log|\tau|>0$. For every $x\in X^{\rm an}$, use the independent-variable Gauss completion of $\mathcal H(x)(T)$ with $|T|=e^{-h}$ and embed $\tau\mapsto T$. The induced point $\sigma(x)\in X_{K'}^{\rm an}$ restricts to $x$. For Laurent sections expanded in a fixed finite $k$-basis,
$$\left|\sum_{r\ge r_0}\tau^r f_r\right|_{\sigma(x)}
 =\max_{r\ge r_0}e^{-rh}|f_r(x)|.\tag{4.4}$$
Independence prevents cancellation even when the chosen radius already lies in the value group of $\mathcal H(x)$. The tails tend uniformly to zero on compact affine charts, proving continuity and consistency on overlaps. This is the Gauss section of BJ Remark 1.9 (S1 LF724--757), with a rescaled rational value-group step.

For a pure FS generating system $s_j\in H^0(X_{K'},mL_{K'})$, flat field base change of $H^0$ gives Laurent expansions $s_j=\sum_{r\ge r_0}\tau^r f_{jr}$ with $f_{jr}\in H^0(X,mL)$. Let $h_0$ be the canonical trivial metric on $L$. Every $k$-section has norm at most one for $h_0$: at the valuation-ring center of $x$ it is regular in a center frame, and its coefficient lies in that valuation ring. Thus the pulled FS potential is
$$\sigma^*\psi=\frac1m\max_{j,r}
 \bigl(\log\|f_{jr}\|_{mh_0}-rh\bigr).\tag{4.5}$$
The left side is finite continuous on compact $X^{\rm an}$ and has a finite lower bound $b$. Every term with $-rh/m<b$ is uniformly below this lower bound, so all sufficiently large $r$ may be removed **exactly**. There are finitely many remaining coefficients. They generate: at a common algebraic zero their terms are all $-\infty$ and the discarded tail is strictly below $b$, contradicting (4.5). All weights $-rh$ are rational. This produces a genuine finite FS metric on the same original $L$; no approximate coefficient cutoff or generic-fiber normalization is involved.

Uniform errors decrease under pullback by $\sigma$. Hence the original continuous metric is a uniform limit of these genuine FS metrics. BE Corollary 7.6, or BJ ample-class decreasing closure, gives genuine membership. Explicitly choose uniform errors $\epsilon_j=4^{-j}$ and shifts
$$B_j=2\sum_{i\ge j}\epsilon_i.$$
If $F_j$ has error $\le\epsilon_j$ relative to the target, then
$$F_j+B_j-(F_{j+1}+B_{j+1})\ge\epsilon_j-\epsilon_{j+1}>0.$$
Thus a same-class decreasing FS sequence is also available for this continuous target. This completes Theorem 4.1.

GM 2.7 alone extends a represented metric from a compact domain, with no preservation of nefness. Theorem 4.1 uses global gluing and all-point curve tests instead. It does not silently replace the needed compact PL extension or bounded product independence in Gate B.

## 5. Canonical determinant weights without flatness

**Theorem 5.1.** Let $k$ be a complete non-Archimedean field of characteristic zero, $A$ a normal integral finitely generated $k$-algebra, and $B$ an integral finite $A$-algebra with $A\hookrightarrow B$. Put $F=\operatorname{Frac}A$, $E=\operatorname{Frac}B$, and $d=[E:F]$. For every $s\in(\operatorname{Spec}A)^{\rm an}$ there are canonical positive integers
$$m_y(s),\qquad y\in\pi^{-1}(s),\qquad \sum_y m_y(s)=d,\tag{5.1}$$
determined by the generic determinant norm. They agree with length times residue degree where $B$ is locally free. They need not equal the dimensions of the nonflat special-fiber algebra factors. Every actual rational AFS input has an actual AFS trace on the whole original base.

### 5.1. Extending the polynomial law, including all relations

For $b_1,\ldots,b_r\in B$, define
$$P(T_1,\ldots,T_r)=\det_F\bigl(\operatorname{mult}_{\sum T_i b_i}:E\otimes_F F[T]\to E\otimes_F F[T]\bigr).\tag{5.2}$$
The universal element is integral over $A[T]$. Over an algebraic closure of $F(T)$ its eigenvalues are the field embeddings of that integral element. Their elementary symmetric functions, including every characteristic-polynomial coefficient, are integral over $A[T]$ and lie in $F[T]\subset F(T)$. Normality of $A[T]$ puts them in $A[T]$. This extends (5.2) across every nonflat base point.

This is a well-defined norm law on special fibers, not just a formula for a chosen tuple. Choose finite $A$-module generators of $B$ and a finite presentation $A^r/R\simeq B$. For any relation vector in $R$, the determinant is invariant under translating its variables by that vector. The identities hold generically, hence coefficientwise in $A$. After tensoring to a field $H$, the kernel of $H^r\to B\otimes_AH$ is the image of $R\otimes_AH$, by right exactness. The translated identities therefore imply well-definedness for every new fiber relation. Multiplicativity, homogeneity of degree $d$, the value $N(1)=1$, and the full Cayley--Hamilton identity also specialize, since they are polynomial identities on finitely many universal module generators. This remains valid if the fiber module has dimension larger than $d$.

### 5.2. Factorization and strict positivity at every fiber point

Put $H=\mathcal H(s)$ and $C=B\otimes_AH$. Over an algebraic closure $\bar H$, write the finite algebra as a product of Artinian local algebras, with residue characters $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_q:C\otimes_H\bar H\to\bar H$ and nilradical $J$. On the unit group the specialized norm is a regular algebraic character. In characteristic zero, the finite polynomial logarithm gives an isomorphism $1+J\simeq(J,+)$ because the algebra is commutative and nilpotent. An additive affine space has no nontrivial regular character into $\mathbb G_m$: a character and its inverse are polynomial functions whose product is one, so both are constant. On the residue torus $(\mathbb G_m)^q$, a regular character is a Laurent monomial. Polynomial extension to the whole algebra makes its exponents nonnegative. Homogeneity gives
$$N_s(c)=\prod_{j=1}^q\chi_j(c)^{n_j},\qquad n_j\ge0,\qquad\sum_j n_j=d.\tag{5.3}$$
For completeness, the equality holds first on the dense unit open and hence as a polynomial on the whole underlying vector space. The torus-character assertion follows by comparing coefficients in $p(xy)=p(x)p(y)$ in the Laurent polynomial ring: a nonzero group-like element has a single monomial with coefficient one.

Every $n_j$ is **strictly positive**. If $n_j=0$, take the idempotent $c$ with residue zero in that factor and residue one in every other factor. Equation (5.3) would give $N_s(c)=1$. The specialized degree-$d$ characteristic polynomial annihilates $c$ and has constant term $(-1)^dN_s(c)\ne0$. Solving that identity for an inverse makes $c$ invertible, which contradicts its zero residue. This also proves why an invisible point cannot be assigned weight zero.

Galois invariance makes $n_j$ equal on the embeddings of each residue field $H_y$ of a local factor of $C$. Characteristic zero makes these finite residue extensions separable. A finite extension of a complete non-Archimedean field has a unique extending absolute value. Set
$$m_y(s)=n_j[H_y:H].\tag{5.4}$$
These are the positive integers of (5.1). They are intrinsic and input-independent. If $B$ is locally free, (5.2) is its ordinary determinant law; an Artinian composition series gives $n_j$ equal to the local Artinian length. There is no local-free hypothesis elsewhere in the argument.

Under any complete field extension of $H$, the residue factors split, with the sum of their new residue degrees equal to the original degree, and their exponents are unchanged. Thus the refined weights aggregate to (5.4). This proves base-change compatibility of weighted sums of any pulled-back function, also for value $-\infty$ when the functions are locally bounded above. It uses the actual specialized polynomial law, rather than an affine regularization theorem over $H$.

### 5.3. Exact AFS formula on the whole base

For (2.1), choose $D$ clearing the $c_i$, put
$$b_0=1,\quad b_i=f_i^{Dc_i},\quad w_0=D\lambda,\quad w_i=DC_i,$$
and expand the actual polynomial
$$P(T)=N\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^rT_i b_i\bigr)=\sum_{|\beta|=d}a_\beta T^\beta\in A[T].$$
Give $T_i$ weighted Gauss radius $e^{w_i}$. The Gauss norm is multiplicative at arbitrary positive real radii. One elementary proof chooses the lexicographically largest maximal-weight monomial in each polynomial: their sum exponent has a unique maximal contribution among maximal-weight terms, and no lower-weight term can cancel it. Apply this after complete algebraic closure and (5.3). Conjugate residue values have equal absolute value. Taking logarithms gives the exact identity
$$N_\pi u(s):=\sum_y m_y(s)u(y)
 =\max_{|\beta|=d}\left(\frac1D\log|a_\beta(s)|+\frac1D\sum_i\beta_iw_i\right).\tag{5.5}$$
The coefficient of $T_0^d$ is one, providing the finite floor $d\lambda$. Zero coefficients are discarded. All other branches use regular functions in the original $A$, so the displayed maximum is continuous everywhere, including the nonflat locus.

To retain any fixed original base generator $g$, express $g$ as a polynomial in the source generators in (2.1). Degree bounds, the positive source slopes, and the finite floor give rational $\eta>0$, $M$ with
$$u\ge\eta\log|g\circ\pi|-M.$$
Since the weights are positive and total $d$, append the dominated branch $d\eta\log|g|-dM$ to (5.5). The value does not change. Doing this for all base generators makes the result an actual AFS, with the original ring and generators. Section 2 supplies its actual ample-reference compactification. Thus “genuine” here has finite algebraic FS data, rather than a tropical inverse-measure meaning.

### 5.4. A nonflat example that separates weight from fiber length

Let $k$ be any characteristic-zero field, $A=k[x,y]$, $I=(x,y)$, and inside $A[z]/(z^2-x)$ let
$$B=A\oplus Iz.$$
Multiplication preserves this finite $A$-module: $(uz)(vz)=xuv\in A$. The ambient quadratic ring is integral, so $B$ is integral and has generic degree two. At the origin,
$$B/(x,y)B\simeq k\oplus (I/(x,y)I)z,$$
which has dimension three, with a two-dimensional square-zero ideal. Hence the finite morphism is not flat there. Nevertheless
$$N(a+uz)=a^2-xu^2,$$
so the specialized norm at the origin is $a(0)^2$. There is one fiber point of canonical weight two, not three.

For original source generators $x,y,xz,yz$, the universal determinant is
$$P=(T_0+xT_1+yT_2)^2-x(xT_3+yT_4)^2.\tag{5.6}$$
At the origin it is $T_0^2$, making an AFS floor $\lambda$ trace to $2\lambda$. Multiplying the special-fiber algebra dimension by that floor would give the wrong $3\lambda$. This is an exact symbolic example, not a numerical sample.

## 6. Whole-base continuity, local integer sums, and finite pullback

**Theorem 6.1.** With the canonical weights of Theorem 5.1, the trace of any continuous real-valued function on $Y^{\rm an}$ is continuous on $S^{\rm an}$. On any compact base set $E$,
$$\|N_\pi a-N_\pi b\|_E\le d\|a-b\|_{\pi^{-1}E}.\tag{6.1}$$
If $u_j\downarrow u$ are actual AFS and $u$ is continuous, then their traces converge locally uniformly, and each trace is an actual AFS on the whole base.

The estimate follows pointwise from positivity and (5.1). A finite morphism is proper, so the inverse image of a compact base neighborhood is compact. Dini's theorem on that compact set applies when the limit is continuous; (6.1) then proves locally uniform convergence of the genuine AFS traces (5.5). This is the required whole-base continuity mechanism for such inputs. It does not infer continuity of a discontinuous bounded-decreasing limit.

For the stronger assertion concerning every continuous input, differences of actual AFS form a rational vector lattice. Positive rational sums and maxima are AFS after distributing the finite maxima and clearing powers. Original generator branches can be appended by (2.2). The identity
$$\max(a-b,c-d)=\max(a+d,c+b)-(b+d)$$
proves lattice closure for differences. On a compact source set, this lattice contains constants in restriction, by moving generator intercepts low enough below a desired floor; it separates seminorms, by truncated log norms of a distinguishing regular function. Arbitrary real scalars can be approximated by rationals on that compact set.

Here is the needed lattice-density proof. For fixed $x,y$ and continuous $f$, choose a lattice function with prescribed values at $x,y$ within a chosen error, using separation, scaling, and constants. For fixed $x$, finitely many such functions, indexed by $y$, have neighborhoods where they exceed $f-\epsilon$ and these neighborhoods cover the compact set. Their maximum exceeds $f-\epsilon$ everywhere and remains below $f+\epsilon$ near $x$. A finite collection of these neighborhoods covers as $x$ varies. The minimum of the corresponding maxima lies between $f-\epsilon$ and $f+\epsilon$ everywhere. It is still in the lattice. Thus differences of AFS uniformly approximate $f$ on the compact set. Their traces are differences of continuous determinant formulas, and (6.1) gives continuity of the limit. This assertion is continuity, not a positivity theorem for arbitrary continuous inputs.

If a continuous input equals one on one clopen fiber piece and zero on the complementary piece over an open base set, its trace is the sum of the canonical positive integer weights in the first piece. Continuity makes this integer sum **locally** constant. It can take different values on different components of that open. This is precisely the conclusion needed for a later shrink around one tested fiber.

Finite pullback also retains original source generators. If $v_j$ is AFS on $S$, its pullback has base branches. Every source generator $z$ satisfies a monic integral equation
$$z^m+\sum_{i<m}b_i z^i=0,$$
whence
$$\log|z|\le\max_{i<m}\frac{\log|b_i|}{m-i}.\tag{6.2}$$
For $z=0$ the statement is immediate. Otherwise, if its norm exceeded every right-hand branch, the leading monomial would have strictly larger norm than every other term, contradicting the equation. Base-generator degree bounds and the positive branches and floor of each $v_j$ let one append a sufficiently small positive $z$-branch with a sufficiently low rational intercept, dominated everywhere. Thus every pulled function is actual AFS on the original $B$, and the decreasing limit is unchanged. The denominator $m-i$ and the source generators are indispensable.

## 7. Radial identification conditional only on open-trace extension

We now retain $k$ algebraically closed, trivially valued, and characteristic zero, $S$ an affine open in $\mathbb A_k^n$, and $Y$ integral affine finite surjective over $S$. Say $u$ has a *contact witness* if it is locally bounded above, is finite at the generic trivial seminorm, and has one proper birational algebraic morphism $\mu:Z\to Y$ such that $u\circ\mu^{\rm an}$ is locally a decreasing sequence of the contact weights of Section 2 on common neighborhoods.

**Theorem 7.1 (conditional extension identification).** Suppose $v$ is an actual AFS-regularizable function on all of $S^{\rm an}$ and, on some dense principal open $W\subset S$ over which $\pi$ is étale and the witness is an isomorphism, $v=N_\pi u$. Then
$$v(s)=\sum_{y\in\pi^{-1}(s)}m_y(s)u(y)\quad\text{for every }s\in S^{\rm an}.\tag{7.1}$$
The hypothesis that such a $v$ exists is retained. It is the open-trace regularization/removal output of Gate B, and is not proved by the determinant formula. The theorem removes the separate residue-field affine-regularization premise from the identification step.

### 7.1. Curve slices agree with the canonical weights

Fix $s$ and set $H=\mathcal H(s)$. The canonical $H$-rational lift $s'$ on $S_H$ has finite fiber $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_AH)$, whose analytic points are exactly the original fiber. Choose a line through $s'$ generically in $W_H$. This exists because $H$ is infinite: for each polynomial defining the complement, its restriction to a line in a variable direction is not identically zero for a direction outside a proper algebraic subset. Intersect with $S_H$ to obtain an affine open of that line.

The scheme-theoretic preimage has pure dimension one. Indeed $Y_H$ is an integral $n$-dimensional finite-type scheme (geometric integrality follows from algebraic closedness of $k$); the $n-1$ line equations give height at most $n-1$ at its components, and finiteness gives dimension at most one. Thus each reduced component dominates the line. Normalize the reduced preimage. The resulting disjoint smooth curves $C$ over the perfect $H$ map finitely and flatly to the line: their coordinate modules are finite torsion-free over the local PIDs of the smooth base curve. Over its generic point in $W_H$ the map is the original étale map, so total rank is $d$.

The generic determinant norm of the source equals the determinant norm on $C$ for every original regular source function, because they agree over that étale open. Both sets of coefficients are regular on the normal line, so the equality holds on the whole line, including the center. Hence (5.3), or uniqueness of its exponents, shows that the length/residue weights of the normalized slice, aggregated over each original fiber point, equal exactly the canonical weights $m_y(s)$. These weights were fixed before the slice or weak input was chosen. Different admissible slices give the same result. No special-fiber dimension from the nonflat source is used.

The generic lift of every component of $C$ through the single witness is defined over the isomorphism open. Properness of $\mu_H$ extends it over the DVR at each missing curve point, and separatedness gives compatible uniqueness. It therefore gives an algebraic map $C\to Z_H$. This is the required local lifting criterion, with its hypotheses checked; arbitrary local analytic curves are not asserted to extend globally.

### 7.2. Direct Gauss limits over the completed residue field

If $H$ is trivially valued, first extend to $H((T))$, with its nontrivial $T$-adic norm. Then in either case pass to a completed algebraic closure $\Omega$. Every original fiber value is preserved under its rational lifts. Pullback of each supplied local contact approximant through the algebraic lift above satisfies Lemma 3.1. Taking the decreasing limit gives a subharmonic function, or the identically $-\infty$ function, on each source curve neighborhood. The actual AFS sequence supplied for $v$ restricts on the base line to finite positive maxima of logs of regular functions and a finite floor, hence gives the same alternative on a base neighborhood. This does not use an AFS approximation theorem over $H$ or $\Omega$.

For a subharmonic function $h$ on a disk about a rational point $0$, harmonic comparison on every sufficiently small closed disk gives
$$h(0)\le h(\xi_R),$$
where $\xi_R$ is its boundary Gauss point. The Gauss points tend to $0$, so upper semicontinuity gives the opposite limsup inequality. Thus
$$\lim_{R\downarrow0}h(\xi_R)=h(0),\tag{7.2}$$
also if $h(0)=-\infty$. For an identically $-\infty$ neighborhood this is immediate.

At a point $x$ of the smooth normalized source curve over the center, choose an analytic coordinate $z$. The finite map has the form
$$t=c z^e U(z),\qquad U(0)=1,\ c\ne0.$$
Here $e$ is a positive integer. Residue characteristic zero ensures that after shrinking, the binomial series for $U^{1/e}$ converges; the coordinate $zU(z)^{1/e}$ has an invertible linear coefficient. The map is therefore exactly $t=cy^e$ on a smaller disk. Finite properness puts every preimage of a sufficiently small target disk in these finitely many source disks.

Choose target radii $R\in|\Omega^\times|$ tending to zero; then $(R/|c|)^{1/e}\in|\Omega^\times|$. Over the target Gauss point there is one source Gauss point in each such disk, of weight $e$. To check the degree, scale the coordinates to radius one: the residual polynomial is $Y^e-\alpha T$ over $\widetilde\Omega(T)$, irreducible by Eisenstein at $T$. A monic reduction argument gives degree $e$ in the completed residue field. The known degree of the disk map and the unique norm extension exclude another point. This is an explicit Gauss-fiber computation, with no punctured-limit assertion.

The complement of $W_H$ on the line is finite. Small noncentral Gauss points therefore lie in $W_H$. At each such point the pulled open identity gives
$$v(\xi_R)=\sum_x e_x (u\circ p)(\xi_{(R/|c_x|)^{1/e_x}}).\tag{7.3}$$
Pass to the limit using (7.2). There are finitely many summands. If one tends to $-\infty$, all others are bounded above on these neighborhoods, so the sum tends to $-\infty$ without subtracting infinities. The central slice weights are the canonical weights by Section 7.1, and residue-field refinements aggregate by Theorem 5.1. Equation (7.1) follows.

Consequently, after Gate B supplies the actual extension $v$, the trace is identified on the **whole** smooth base and is compatible with the single original witness. Combined with Section 6, it gives the local integer sums, degree estimate, and actual finite pullback needed by the conditional split-piece proof. It does not by itself supply that extension or the singular envelope theorem.

## 8. Bounded local products and the remaining smooth gate

Theorem 4.1 removes the representation and positivity circularity for its explicit continuous contact metrics. The following construction proves a bounded local product statement for that exact decreasing class. It does not accept the embedded round70 chain by citation.

The literal CLD Proposition 8.7.2 assumes continuous functions converging **locally uniformly**. ## 2. The actual global operator and the equation reduction

Write $n=\dim X$, $\omega=c_1(L)$ and $V=(L^n)>0$. Let $\operatorname{PSH}(X,\omega)$ always mean BJ's genuine global generated cone, not the corrected auxiliary local cone introduced later. For this section geometric unibranchness is unnecessary. Irreducibility gives the one-constant uniqueness statement. BJ also treats ample real numerical Cartier classes; the original line-bundle target suffices here.

### 2.1. Model geometry retains a nonnormal generic fiber

BJ v4 LF450--469 defines varieties to be reduced, with no normality assumption. Section 7 explicitly resumes general projective varieties at LF3649--3658. This scope is decisive: there is a genuine singular-space operator already in the source.

On a test configuration $\mathcal X\to\mathbb A^1$, integral closure means closure **inside its prescribed generic fiber**. On an affine chart $A$, close $A$ in $A\otimes_{k[t]}k(t)$. BJ Definition 1.10, Example 1.11 and Theorem 1.13, LF759--849, prove finiteness and the vertical $R_1,S_2$ criterion. Absolute normalization would change a nonnormal generic fiber and is not substituted.

Here is the relevant mechanism in the proof. A vertical fractional ideal has poles only on the central fiber. At an associated polar point, an element $f$ satisfies $f\mathfrak m\mathfrak a\subset A$ but $f\mathfrak a\not\subset A$. If the former ideal lies in $\mathfrak m$, the determinant trick would make $f\mathfrak a$ integral and hence regular, a contradiction. Otherwise $f\mathfrak m\mathfrak a=A$, making $\mathfrak m$ invertible, so the point is a DVR. Conversely vertical depth at least two rules out a higher-codimension associated pole, while the vertical DVRs rule out codimension-one poles. This is a replacement for absolute normality, not a smoothness assumption.

For a central component $E$, let $b_E=\operatorname{ord}_E(t)>0$ and $v_E=b_E^{-1}\operatorname{ord}_E|_{k(X)}$. With relatively nef model data $\theta_{i,\mathcal X}+D_i$, the actual raw mixed measure is
$$
 M^{\mathrm{raw}}((\theta_1,\phi_1),\ldots,(\theta_n,\phi_n))
 =\sum_E b_E\prod_{i=1}^n((\theta_{i,\mathcal X}+D_i)|_E)\,\delta_{v_E}. \tag{2.1}
$$
The product denotes an intersection number, including the central fundamental cycle. Nefness gives nonnegative weights. Rational equivalence of the central and generic fibers gives total mass $(\theta_1\cdots\theta_n)_X$. In particular the diagonal raw mass is $V$, not one. The factor $b_E$ cannot be suppressed.

### 2.2. Energy and Radon representation

The compactified intersection pairing is symmetric and independent of determination by the projection formula. Translating its $i$th potential by $c$ adds $c(\prod_{j\ne i}\theta_j)_X$. BJ 7.1 extends it as the infimum over model majorants. Monotonicity follows from nef intersections. To verify upper semicontinuity, choose a majorant tuple below a prescribed strict pairing threshold. The functionals $\sup(\phi_i-\psi_i)$ are continuous in BJ's divisorial topology, so small translated majorants remain above all nearby potentials. The translation rule controls their pairing. This proves upper semicontinuity and decreasing-net continuity; it uses no envelope property.

BJ 7.8--7.14 extend the finite mixed pairing by multilinearity to differences of finite-energy potentials. Ample class comparisons and the expansion of the energy of sums ensure that the requisite mixed terms are finite. Define
$$
 E_\omega(\phi)=\frac{\langle(\omega,\phi)^{n+1}\rangle}{(n+1)V},\qquad
 \mathcal E^1(X,\omega)=\{\phi\in\operatorname{PSH}(X,\omega):E_\omega(\phi)>-\infty\}.
 \tag{2.2}
$$
We have $E(0)=0$, $E(\phi+c)=E(\phi)+c$, and $E$ is increasing, concave, upper semicontinuous and decreasing-continuous.

For a genuine algebraic PL test $a$, set
$$
 \int a\,dM^{\mathrm{raw}}
 =\langle(0,a),(\theta_1,\phi_1),\ldots,(\theta_n,\phi_n)\rangle. \tag{2.3}

For affine $Y=\operatorname{Spec}A$ define actual rational affine FS functions (AFS) to be

where all displayed constants and positive coefficients are rational and the list of regular $f_i$ contains algebra generators of $A$. A generating system for a finite-dimensional space or a list of powers alone is insufficient. Upper growth means $u\le H+C$ for some AFS $H$.

A corrected continuous rational local contact function is a finite continuous selection from finitely many rational affine expressions in regular log norms on finite local charts. A contact support satisfies $b(s)\ge\ell(s)+C$ and $b(t)=\ell(t)+C$, with the **same** constant. At an infinite tropical coordinate, the support and every branch used on its finite chart must have zero coefficient in that coordinate; shrink so all remaining used functions are units. Positive rational sums and maxima of AFS functions are AFS after distributing their finite maxima and clearing rational exponents into regular monomials. ## 4. Explicit strict barriers and real logarithmic supports

### 4.1. A strict support gap on extended tropical coordinates

Let $T_N=(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})^N$. Choose an integer $a\ge\log(N+1)$ and set
$$\chi_N(t)=a^{-1}\log\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-at_i}\right),\quad e^{-a\infty}=0. \tag{4.1}$$
It is continuous on $T_N$, convex and coordinatewise decreasing on the finite part, and
$$\max(0,-t_1,\ldots,-t_N)\le\chi_N(t)
 \le\max(0,-t_1,\ldots,-t_N)+1. \tag{4.2}$$
Fix $t$. Let $I$ be its finite-coordinate set, $Z=1+\sum_{i\in I}e^{-at_i}$, $p_0=1/Z$ and $p_i=e^{-at_i}/Z$ for $i\in I$. Define
$$\ell_t(s)=\chi_N(t)-\sum_{i\in I}p_i(s_i-t_i). \tag{4.3}$$
At a pole $s_i=\infty$ for $i\in I$, give this support value $-\infty$. Its other coefficients are zero. The convex support inequality gives $\chi_N\ge\ell_t$. Equality occurs only at $s=t$: the Hessian in the finite $I$ coordinates is $a(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^T)$, positive definite since $p_0>0$; any finite value in a formerly infinite coordinate strictly increases (4.1).

We prove the global gap, not just strict pointwise contact. In finite $I$ coordinates the gap is bounded below by
$$\max(0,-s_i:i\in I)+\sum_{i\in I}p_i s_i-C_t.$$
The homogeneous part is positive on every nonzero vector: its first term is the maximum of $0,-s_i$, and the negative of its second term is a strict weighted average of those values, with all weights $p_i,p_0$ positive. Compactness of the unit sphere gives coercivity. A bounded gap sublevel therefore confines these coordinates to a bounded interval. The gap bound and bounded support then give a lower bound for the other coordinates; their upper endpoint $\infty$ is allowed. Gap sublevels are closed and compact in the extended product; when a used coordinate tends to $\infty$ the gap tends to $+\infty$. The zero set is exactly $\{t\}$. In any compact gap sublevel, the complement of a neighborhood of $t$ has a positive minimum. Outside that sublevel the gap is already uniformly positive. Hence, for every neighborhood $V$ of $t$, there is $\delta>0$ with
$$\chi_N(s)-\ell_t(s)\ge\delta\quad(s\notin V). \tag{4.4}$$
If $I$ is empty, the support is zero; (4.1) directly bounds every coordinate below on a gap sublevel, and the same argument applies. This proves the full extended-coordinate statement without the printed Gaussian-extension argument.

### 4.2. Uniform multinomial AFS approximants

Put $z_0=1$, $z_i=e^{-at_i}$. Expanding $(\sum_{i=0}^N z_i)^m$ gives $B_m=\binom{m+N}{N}$ nonnegative summands. Their maximum lies between the sum divided by $B_m$ and the sum. Thus
$$q_m(t)=\max_{|\beta|=m}\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\beta_i}{m}t_i
 +\frac{\log\binom m\beta}{am}\right\}$$
satisfies
$$q_m\le\chi_N\le q_m+\frac{\log B_m}{am} \tag{4.5}$$
on the entire extended product. Terms meeting a pole have value $-\infty$; the $\beta_0=m$ term is the zero floor. After composition $t_i=-\log|f_i|$, the regular monomial is $\prod f_i^{\beta_i}$ and its log coefficient is $1/m$. If the $f_i$ contain generators, the terms $\beta_i=1$, $\beta_0=m-1$ contain those generators themselves.

Choose $m_j$ with the error in (4.5) at most $\epsilon_j/4$, round every finite intercept upward to rationals with error at most $\epsilon_j/4$, and add rational $\epsilon_j$, where $\epsilon_{j+1}\le\epsilon_j/4$. The resulting AFS value is between $\chi_N+3\epsilon_j/4$ and $\chi_N+5\epsilon_j/4$. Consequently the sequence decreases everywhere and converges to $\chi_N$. This is global uniform approximation, including poles.

### 4.3. Real supports require individual floors

Let $p_i>0$ be arbitrary real coefficients, $C\in\mathbb R$, and $f_i$ regular. Choose rational AFS $H\ge1$ containing the original generators and integers $D_i\ge1$ with $\log|f_i|\le D_iH$. Define
$$F_{ij}=\max(\log|f_i|,2^{-j}H-j). \tag{4.6}$$
These are actual AFS, decrease to the individual logs, and obey $F_{ij}\le D_iH$. Choose nested rational intervals $0\le q_{ij}\le p_i\le r_{ij}$, with $q_{ij}\uparrow p_i$ and $r_{ij}\downarrow p_i$, and rational $C_j\downarrow C$. Put
$$\eta_j=\sum_iD_i(r_{ij}-q_{ij}),\qquad
 L_j=\sum_iq_{ij}F_{ij}+(\eta_j+2^{-j})H+C_j. \tag{4.7}$$
For nonzero $f_i$ at the point, replacing $p_i$ by $q_{ij}$ costs at most $D_i(p_i-q_{ij})H$; negative logs only improve this inequality. Thus $L_j\ge\sum p_i\log|f_i|+C$. At a pole the inequality is immediate. Monotonicity is exact:
$$\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge\sum_iD_i(q_{i,j+1}-q_{ij}).$$
Expand $L_j-L_{j+1}$, use $F_{ij}\ge F_{i,j+1}$ and $F_{i,j+1}\le D_iH$, and the displayed inequality gives a nonnegative result. The positive $2^{-j}H$ term and the individual lower bounds in (4.6) retain generator growth; after distribution low generator branches can be appended as in Section 3. Therefore $L_j$ are actual AFS.

At a fixed point all nonpole terms have finite limits. If some $p_i>0$ and $f_i=0$, then $q_{ij}$ is eventually positive and $q_{ij}F_{ij}\to-\infty$, while the other terms are bounded above. Thus the limit is the desired support even on its $-\infty$ locus. Omit zero coefficients entirely.

The individual floors are essential. On $\mathbb A^2_{z,w}$, the function $\max(p\log|z|,-j)$ is constantly $-j$ along $z=0$, even as $|w|\to\infty$. It cannot contain a positive retained $w$-generator branch. Flooring the entire singular sum loses precisely that growth; (4.6) does not.

### 4.4. Countable strict potentials and an explicit diagonal

Suppose $k$ is countable, algebraically closed and trivially valued. Enumerate its affine coordinate algebra and retain embedding generators in every list. These finite tropicalizations generate the analytic topology. For an AFS exhaustion $H\ge1$, degree bounds and (4.2) allow positive rational $\gamma_j$ such that
$$0\le\gamma_j\chi_{N_j}\circ\operatorname{Trop}_j\le2^{-j}(H+1).$$
The sum $\rho=\sum_j\gamma_j\chi_{N_j}\circ\operatorname{Trop}_j$ is continuous by uniform convergence on each generator-bounded compact, and has upper logarithmic growth. To prove actual decreasing AFS regularization, set
$$T_r=\sum_{j\le r}\gamma_j\chi_{N_j}\circ\operatorname{Trop}_j+2^{-r}(H+1).$$
The functions $T_r$ decrease. Approximate each finite sum uniformly on the whole affine space by an AFS $A_r$ with error $\epsilon_r=4^{-r}$ using (4.5), and put $B_r=2\sum_{i\ge r}\epsilon_i$. Then $A_r+B_r$ decreases, since its consecutive difference is at least $2\epsilon_r-\epsilon_r-\epsilon_{r+1}>0$. Its limit is $\rho$.

For $x\in Y^{\mathrm{an}}$ and a neighborhood $B$, a finite tropicalization has an inverse-image neighborhood contained in $B$. Replace its one $\chi$ summand by (4.3). The resulting $\rho'$ satisfies
$$\rho'\le\rho,\qquad \rho'(x)=\rho(x),\qquad
 \rho'\le\rho-\delta\ \text{outside }B. \tag{4.8}$$
It has an actual decreasing AFS sequence. For $r$ beyond the replaced index, approximate the remaining finite continuous summands as above, replace the fixed support by its **decreasing** sequence (4.7), retain the tail $2^{-r}(H+1)$, and add $B_r$. Consecutive differences are nonnegative from the decreasing support and the preceding error estimate. The other summands stay bounded above at each pole of the support, proving the correct extended limit. This explicit diagonal avoids any unsupported uniform approximation of a real support at its logarithmic poles. The construction is a countable auxiliary theorem, not an arbitrary-cardinality envelope theorem.

$$a\max(-\operatorname{ord}_Dh,0)\le c\operatorname{ord}_Df. \tag{5.2}$$
Outside $Z(f)$, $h$ is regular. For positive integers $p,q$ with $q/p>c/a$, (5.2) shows that $z=h^pf^q$ has no height-one poles. $$f^Nz^l=f^{N+ql}h^{pl}\in A\quad(l\ge1). \tag{5.3}$$

Let $L_0\subset Y_f^{\mathrm{an}}$ be compact and let $x\in\widehat L_{0,Y}\cap Y_f^{\mathrm{an}}$, where the hull is defined using **the original ring $A$**. Suppose $|\log|f||\le M$ on $L_0\cup\{x\}$. Use (5.3) as actual regular hull tests. When $h(x)\ne0$ and $\sup_{L_0}|h|>0$, dividing the log inequality by $pl$, then letting $l\to\infty$, gives
$$a\log|h(x)|+b\le\sup_{L_0}(a\log|h|+b)+2a(q/p)M.$$
Let $q/p\downarrow c/a$ to obtain
$$a\log|h(x)|+b\le\sup_{L_0}(a\log|h|+b)+2cM. \tag{5.4}$$
If $h(x)=0$ this is immediate. If $h$ vanishes on all of $L_0$, the regular tests (5.3) force $h(x)=0$ because $f(x)\ne0$. No subtraction of infinities is used.

Denominator exponent counting is invalid. In $A=k[z]$, take $f=z^2$, $h=z^{-1}=z/f$, $a=2,c=1$, and $U=\max(0,2\log|z|)$. ## 6. The repaired split-piece implication

This section is a conditional mathematical theorem. Its antecedents are stated to prevent an unreviewed generated proof from being silently accepted.

**Metric antecedent.** An actual AFS reference admits a rational ample compactification whose affine chart is the original affine variety and whose local weight is that reference. A continuous rational contact compact perturbation of such a reference has an actual decreasing AFS sequence. Continuous glued rational ample metrics with a whole reference-winning collar are genuinely global PSH; decreasing closure and already-genuine same-ample-class sequential FS regularization, with exact section/generator conversion, are available. Controlled approximation in the precise form used for (5.5) is available. No upper-envelope property on a singular target is included.

**Smooth antecedent.** Smooth upper-growth weak affine regularization and principal-open removal are proved using target-side smooth EP, including equality of the removed-set values on the original witness.

**Trace antecedent.** For finite surjective $\pi:Y\to S$, with $Y$ integral affine and $S$ a smooth affine open of $\mathbb A^n$, there are input-independent positive integer weights $m_y(s)$ on every finite analytic fiber, summing to the generic degree $d$. Every weak upper-growth input with a single proper witness has an AFS-regularizable trace
$$N_\pi u(s)=\sum_{y\in\pi^{-1}(s)}m_y(s)u(y). \tag{6.1}$$
For genuine AFS tests this is the actual determinant norm extended over the normal base, hence continuous everywhere. The weights include the correct slicing and residue contributions; on a nonflat fiber they are not assumed to equal arbitrary special-fiber algebra dimensions. ### 6.1. Rossi and the localized hull implication

$$ (u+c\rho)(x)\le\sup_L(u+c\rho)\quad(x\in\widehat L_Y\setminus Z^{\mathrm{an}}). \tag{6.3}$$

## 2. Signed quotient norms

Let homogeneous algebra generators $g_i$ (redundant elements are allowed) have arbitrary assigned real weights $\lambda_i$. In $R_\alpha$ let $F^a$ be the span of monomials of weight $\alpha$ whose assigned weight is at least $a$. Define $\chi(f)$ as the largest such index, and use the minimum over homogeneous components for nonhomogeneous elements. A positive Reeb degree bounds all eligible exponents, so there are finitely many eligible monomials in a fixed weight space. All indices are finite and attained; relations are retained in the quotient filtration. Addition and multiplication of expressions give the norm inequalities and
$$
 \min_i\frac{\lambda_i}{d_\theta(g_i)}d_\theta(\alpha)
 \leq\chi(f)\leq\max_i\frac{\lambda_i}{d_\theta(g_i)}d_\theta(\alpha).                            \tag{14}
$$
Replacing $\lambda_i$ by the actual $\chi(g_i)$ leaves the filtration unchanged. Increasing assignments gives one inclusion. For the other, multiplicativity puts every newly assigned monomial in the old filtration at its new index. An expression attaining the old index cannot acquire a strictly larger minimum new index, since that would increase $\chi(f)$. This verifies the saturation required by B Definition 3.6.

The exact potential identity is
$$ \sup_{f\in R_\alpha\setminus0,\ \alpha\ne0}\frac{\chi(f)-v(f)}{d_\theta(\alpha)}
       =\max_i\frac{\lambda_i-v(g_i)}{d_\theta(g_i)}.                                        \tag{15}$$
For the upper inequality choose an expression attaining $\chi(f)$ and a term with minimum valuation. Then $\chi(f)-v(f)$ is at most that term's assigned weight minus valuation. Division by its common degree makes it a weighted average of generator branches. The reverse inequality uses $f=g_i$ and $\chi(g_i)\geq\lambda_i$. If every term has infinite value the upper bound is trivial; otherwise use a finite-valued minimum term. No cancellation is presumed absent.

An arbitrary primary list can be supplemented by the fixed $h_i$ at sufficiently negative weights without changing its function on any prescribed compact Reeb neighborhood. On $K$ some primary element has value zero, giving a uniform lower bound $-B$ for that list on the neighborhood. Appending $h_i$ with weight $-M$, where $M\geq B\max_{\theta,i}d_\theta(\beta_i)$, puts every added branch below $-B$. Equality on $K$ implies equality everywhere. The representation parameter $M$ may depend on the list; the estimates (2),(3) do not.

For rational assignments, clear indices by $b$ to obtain the integer Rees algebra
$$ \Gamma=\bigoplus_{q,a}t^{-a}F^a_{b\chi}R_q=k[t,g_it^{-b\lambda_i}]\subset R[t,t^{-1}].            \tag{16}$$
Filtered spanning expressions prove the equality also for negative weights. At real weights no integer-Noetherian Rees assertion is made. A valid real degree shift is
$$ \chi_{a,\theta}(f)=\chi(f)+a d_\theta(\alpha).                                                \tag{17}$$
Every expression receives the same shift, so it is exactly the quotient norm with shifted assignments. Negation is not valid: assigning $x,x^2$ both weight $-1$ in $k[x]$ gives $\chi(x)=\chi(x^2)=-1$, and $-\chi$ is not multiplicative.

Let $N_\theta(m)$ be the cutoff dimension, $W_\theta^\chi(m)$ the signed spectral sum on it, and $D_\theta(m)$ the sum of Reeb degrees with their dimensions. An adapted basis gives the finite identity
$$ W_\theta^{\chi_{a,\theta}}(m)=W_\theta^\chi(m)+aD_\theta(m),\qquad
 D_\theta(m)=mN_\theta(m)-\int_0^mN_\theta(r)\,dr.                                              \tag{18}$$
If $N\sim Vm^n/n!$, splitting the integral at a fixed large cutoff proves $D/(mN)\to n/(n+1)$. Shifts are added back only in their **own degree**, not in a different field's degree.

## 3. The effective rational quotient

For rational $\eta$ write $\eta=s\eta_e$, where the supported integer grading of $\eta_e$ has gcd one. Only this effective grading matters; primitiveness in an ineffective ambient torus is insufficient. A normal good cone is integral: its normal components are disjoint, while the positive grading contracts every component to the one vertex.

Take $d$ sufficiently divisible so that $A=R^{(d)}$ and the degree-Veronese of (16) are generated in new degree one, and put $V=\operatorname{Proj}R$, $L_d=\mathcal O_V(d)$. The generation assertion follows without a weighted-degree assumption: choose $d_0$ divisible by all positive generator degrees, extract powers of degree $d_0$, and leave exponents below these powers. The residual monomials have bounded degree $B_0$. Choose a multiple $d>B_0$ of $d_0$. For a monomial of degree $rd$, the residual degree is divisible by $d_0$; combine it with enough extracted blocks to have degree $d$, then partition the remaining blocks into degree-$d$ groups. This works over $k[t]$ as well as $k$. Quotients inherit generation. Enlarge $d$ further to avoid the finite low-degree discrepancy between a finitely generated graded algebra and sections on its relative Proj: the localization description and Serre vanishing give equality in all sufficiently high degrees, and this further Veronese puts every positive degree there. Low-degree differences alone would not change a leading spectral mean.

The ring $A=R^{\mu_d}$ is finite in $R$, since each generator has its $d$th power in $A$. It is normal: an element of $\operatorname{Frac}A$ integral over $A$ belongs to $R$ by normality, and invariance puts it in $A$. The degree gcd makes $\mu_d$ faithful. Its invariant field is $\operatorname{Frac}A$ (multiply a denominator by the other conjugates). The elementary fixed-field theorem for a faithful finite group, proved by independence of its distinct field automorphisms, gives
$$ [\operatorname{Frac}R:\operatorname{Frac}A]=d. $$
All residues occur: the semigroup of generator degrees has gcd one and contains every sufficiently large integer. To see the last assertion, fix a generator degree $q$, choose a nonnegative degree representative of each residue modulo $q$, and add multiples of $q$. Nonzero products witness these degrees in the domain.

On a new degree-one element $a$, $A[a^{-1}]=A[a^{-1}]_0[a,a^{-1}]$. Thus $V$ is normal, and the punctured standard cone is the **actual** $L_d^{-1}$ torsor. For $n\geq2$, normal Hartogs across the codimension-$n$ vertex yields
$$ A_l=H^0(V,lL_d).                                                                            \tag{19}$$
Indeed a normal noetherian domain is the intersection of its height-one local rings, and none of those points has been removed. Functions on the torsor therefore extend, and taking homogeneous pieces gives (19). In dimension one, degree-zero homogeneous fractions form the field of the integral projective point $\operatorname{Proj}R$, hence $k$. A homogeneous fraction $z$ of degree one exists by the degree gcd. Every homogeneous element is a scalar multiple of a power of $z$, so $R=k[z^S]$ for a positive monoid of gcd one. Normality saturates $S$ in $\mathbb Z$, forcing $S=\mathbb N$. Thus $R=k[z]$ and the quotient is a point. This treats that case without Hartogs or a nonexistent curve.

Restriction of (15) to $A$ has exactly the same supremum after degree conversion. The full supremum gives its upper bound; powers of every generator lying in $A$ give its lower bound, even if those powers have saturated norm larger than their assigned weight. Equivalently raise each primary branch to a common degree $D$ divisible by $d$; its coefficient must become $(D/q_i)\lambda_i$. Leaving its coefficient unchanged would not give (20).

After intersecting with the $p-1$ remaining nef classes, put $q_{ij}=(E_iE_j\mathcal L_2\cdots\mathcal L_p)$. For $i\ne j$, proper effective intersections and nefness give $q_{ij}\geq0$. The fiber divisor is pulled back from the base, so $\sum_jb_jq_{ij}=0$; its line bundle is trivial on each $E_i$. Consequently
$$ D^2\mathcal L_2\cdots\mathcal L_p
 =-\sum_{i<j}b_ib_jq_{ij}\left(\frac{r_i}{b_i}-\frac{r_j}{b_j}\right)^2\leq0. $$
A resolution may be chosen with a normal-crossing central support in characteristic zero; the projection formula returns this inequality to the original determination. For $p=0$ the energy is linear. For $p\geq1$, differentiation of the $(p+1)$-fold energy intersection along a segment gives $p$ times this nonpositive mixed vertical pairing divided by $(L^p)$. This proves concavity on rational model segments. Uniform FS approximation and continuity give it on all rational CPSH segments. Simultaneous root approximants transfer these identities to arbitrary fields using the bounded current convergence. Convex combinations and maxima are actual CPSH there: at rational fields products of section lists give positive sums; for irrational fields approximate by rational fields, form these combinations, and root back to the fixed field.
